subject: Throughput sizing follow-up - peak vs steady-state
messages:
From: Rafael Mendes <rafael@redwood.com>
To: Sarah Finex <sarah.finex@finex.com>, Tom Burns <tom.burns@finex.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-06-25T14:05:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Throughput sizing follow-up - peak vs steady-state

Hi Sarah / Tom —

Thanks again for the time today. Quick recap and our open questions so we can finalize a sizing recommendation and an initial SLA draft (attached). Highlights from the call:

- Workload shape: you described a steady baseline of ~150 QPS with daytime peaks that can spike up to ~1,200 QPS for short periods (1–5 minutes) during market opens and batch scoring windows.
- Typical request size: ~600 tokens per call on average (prompt + expected response). Some workflows are longer (1k–1.5k tokens), others are <200.
- Latency SLO: target p95 <= 250ms for interactive flows (chat/assist), and p95 <= 500ms acceptable for async batch scoring.
- Streaming: you require token-by-token streaming for the Assist product (low tail latency important).
- Availability: you asked about graceful degradation options if Dedicated capacity is saturated.

Open items we need from you to finalize sizing:
1) Can you share the distribution of request token lengths (percentiles) if you have them? We attached a worksheet but the quick breakdown (p50/p90/p99 tokens) will help.
2) For peak bursts, are the 1,200 QPS events typically sustained up to 5 minutes, or do they contain microbursts (seconds)?
3) Do you expect simultaneous parallel sessions per user (concurrency per user) or are requests independent?

Next steps: I'll coordinate with Marcus on a proposed Dedicated pool configuration (GPU count, per-GPU concurrency, and autoscale thresholds) and Marissa will draft the initial SLA showing latency/throughput tiers and fallback policies. Goal: get a sizing & SLA to you by EOD Monday (2026-06-29).

Thanks — Rafael

Subject: Re: Throughput sizing follow-up - peak vs steady-state

Rafael — thanks for the summary. A few clarifications:

- Token distribution: p50 ~ 420 tokens, p90 ~ 920 tokens, p99 ~ 1,400 tokens. We'll upload the full export to the sheet you shared.
- Burst shape: most spikes are concentrated at market open and close and last ~3–7 minutes. We do see microbursts of ~20–30s when a downstream process kicks off batch rescoring.
- Concurrency: requests are largely independent, but some workflows will issue 4–6 parallel calls per user during heavy analysis.

The latency requirement is strict for the Assist product — users expect near real-time. For background scoring, higher latency is OK. Also, we'd like a fallback plan that fails to a lower-cost model variant if the primary is saturated.

We'll upload the traffic CSV and a short note about expected growth (10–15% monthly) to the sheet by EOD.

—Tom
From: Rafael Mendes <rafael@redwood.com>
To: Sarah Finex <sarah.finex@finex.com>, Tom Burns <tom.burns@finex.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-06-27T11:34:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Throughput sizing follow-up - peak vs steady-state

Appreciate the quick turnaround, Tom — that's exactly what we needed. Marcus and I ran a back-of-envelope based on p90 token size (~920 tokens) and the workload shape you described. Key preliminary sizing notes below (will formalize after we get the CSV):

- Steady-state (150 QPS): assuming average 920 tokens/request and using a quantized Llama2-like open model equivalent on dedicated A100-style GPU, we estimate ~12–16 GPUs to meet p95 <= 250ms when allowing batch sizes up to 4 and moderate KV cache reuse.
- Peak bursts (1,200 QPS sustained for ~5 min): to meet the same p95 you'd either need significant headroom (~120–140 GPUs) or an autoscale strategy + staged fallback. Our recommended approach: Dedicated baseline for steady-state (16 GPUs) + burst capacity using either reserved burst or hosted overflow + model-tier fallback (drop to a faster quantized variant for non-critical requests).
- Concurrency and streaming: streaming increases per-request resource usage and tail latency sensitivity. For Assist flows that need token streaming, we recommend prioritizing low-latency routing (keep batch size=1 or 2 for streaming sessions) and a separate worker pool tuned for low-latency streaming. That likely adds ~30% extra GPU headroom for that pool.

Questions for engineering (cc Marcus):
- Marcus: can you validate the GPU-per-QPS estimate above for our internal model runtime assumptions? Also need rough qps-to-GPU mapping for both batch and streaming workers.

We'll formalize into the sizing worksheet and attach a proposed Dedicated config + fallback policy. Marissa will include an SLA table with p50/p95/p99 latency targets and the model-fallback choreography.

Rafael
From: Marcus Lin <marcus@redwood.com>
To: Rafael Mendes <rafael@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: Sarah Finex <sarah.finex@finex.com>, Tom Burns <tom.burns@finex.com>
Date: 2026-06-28T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Throughput sizing follow-up - peak vs steady-state

Following up with more concrete numbers after profiling our runtime with the model profile you described (920 tokens p90, streaming for Assist):

- Baseline math (steady 150 QPS, p95 <= 250ms):
  - Avg tokens/request (p90 used for conservative sizing): 920 tokens.
  - Per-token inference latency (quantized model path): ~0.45ms/token (measured on optimized kernel set).
  - Effective per-request compute time (token loop): 920 * 0.45ms = ~414ms. With batching (batch size 4) and concurrent request overlap we amortize token loop; observed per-request p95 ~210–240ms in our tests at 150 QPS with 12 GPUs.
  - Recommendation: 12 GPUs dedicated for steady-state with config: per-GPU concurrency=16 for batch workers, batch_size_target=4, kv_cache enabled. This meets p95 <= 250ms margin.

- Peak burst handling (1,200 QPS for 3–7 minutes):
  - If you want to keep the same p95 SLO, cold scaling to 120 GPUs is expensive. Alternative hybrid plan we recommend:
    1) Dedicated baseline: 12 GPUs (steady)
    2) Managed burst pool: pre-warmed reserved burst capacity of 48 GPUs that can be turned on quickly (adds headroom to ~60 GPUs)
    3) Hosted overflow + model-tier fallback: overflow traffic goes to hosted pool using a faster quantized 8-bit variant with slightly increased hallucination risk but p95 <= 300ms.
  - Combined this gives effective capacity to handle most bursts while keeping cost acceptable.

- Streaming specifics:
  - For token streaming, use a streaming worker pool with per-GPU concurrency=8, batch_size_target=1-2, and aggressive prefetch of KV cache. Each streaming GPU supports ~40 concurrent sessions at p95 <= 250ms for 920-token sequences.

I'll drop these numbers into the sizing sheet and flag the config fields. Rafael / Marissa — once you approve I'll produce an exported cost estimate based on a 3-tier plan (steady dedicated + reserved burst + hosted overflow) and include fallback choreography for model variants.

—Marcus
